title: Counting Bits
statement:
A permissions service stores each role as an integer bitmask, one bit per permission. For a dashboard it wants a lookup table: for every mask value from 0 to n, how many permissions (1 bits) does it grant?

Write def solution(n) that returns a list ans of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary form of i. Aim for O(n) total time: reuse earlier answers instead of counting each number's bits from scratch.

examples.why: The LeetCode 338 example 1. 0, 1 and 10 in binary.
The LeetCode 338 example 2. 3 is 11 and 5 is 101, so both have count 2.
Only the number 0, which has no 1 bits.

think.a: One entry per number 0, 1, ..., n: its popcount, the count of 1s in its binary form. For example 5 is 101, so ans[5] = 2. The list has n + 1 entries, and ans[0] = 0.

think.q: Write 0 to 8 in binary next to their counts. Do you see a link between i and i // 2?
think.a: 0 0 0, 1 1 1, 2 10 1, 3 11 2, 4 100 1, 5 101 2, 6 110 2, 7 111 3, 8 1000 1. Dropping the last bit of 6 (110) gives 3 (11), and 6 has the same count because the dropped bit was 0. Dropping the last bit of 7 gives 3 too, and 7 has one more, because the dropped bit was 1.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: For each i, test its bits one by one (i & 1, then shift right) and count. A number up to 100,000 has 17 bits, so this is O(n log n). It is fine, but it ignores that the answer for i is almost the answer for a smaller number you already have.

Bit tricks plus a tiny DP. i >> 1 is i without its last bit, and i & 1 is that last bit. So ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), and i >> 1 < i is already filled in. Another version: ans[i] = ans[i & (i - 1)] + 1, because i & (i - 1) clears the lowest 1 bit. Both are O(1) per number.
n = 0 (answer [0], not []). n = 1. Powers of two, which have a count of 1. Numbers like 7, 15, 31 (all ones). An off-by-one that returns n entries instead of n + 1.

hints: Write 0 to 8 in binary. How does the bit count of i relate to the count of i // 2?
Shifting right by one drops the last bit. The count only changes by that last bit: 0 or 1.
ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), filled from i = 1 upward, because i >> 1 is always smaller than i.
explain:
Example 2, n = 5:

  • ans[0] = 0.
  • i = 1 (1): ans[0] + 1 = 1.
  • i = 2 (10): ans[1] + 0 = 1.
  • i = 3 (11): ans[1] + 1 = 2.
  • i = 4 (100): ans[2] + 0 = 1.
  • i = 5 (101): ans[2] + 1 = 2.

Result [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2]. Every step reads one earlier entry and adds one bit, so the whole table costs O(n). In Python, bin(i).count('1') (or i.bit_count() in 3.10+) also works and is fast in practice, but in an interview the point is the recurrence.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output

tests.why: one entry, not an empty list
